1.pericope_label: Moreover Josiah kept a passover unto the Lord in Jerusalem: and they killed the passover on the fourteenth day of the first month. And he set the priests in their charges, and encouraged them to the service of the house of the Lord, And said unto the Levites that taught all Israel, which were holy unto the Lord, Put the holy ark in the house which Solomon the son of David king of Israel did build; it shall not be a burden upon your shoulders: serve now the Lord your God, and his people Israel,

schools.summary: Delitzsch treats the first verse as a heading, marks the fourteenth day of the first month as exactly the time the law fixed — pointedly unlike Hezekiah's passover — maps the chapter's four movements, and reads the command about the ark as ending the Levites' portage duty rather than restoring a displaced ark; Ellicott renders the priests' charges literally as their wards, glosses holy to the Lord as separated to his service, and takes the command about the ark to imply it had been removed from the inner sanctuary.

Gill notes that Jerusalem was the only lawful place for the feast, describes the Levites' teaching office as going through the tribes to instruct the people in God's word and worship, and reports an old manuscript that reads the phrase quite differently, as those who prepared the holy things for all Israel.

Clarke supposes the priests had themselves secured the ark when they saw the idolatrous kings destroying whatever might lead the people back to the true God, and that it could be returned now the reform was settled.

Henry explains the proportions of the two histories, the older giving length to the destruction of the idols and this book to the feast, and places the passover as chief of all the appointed feasts — opening them on the night Israel left Egypt and closing them on the night Christ was betrayed — before carrying the point forward to the Lord's supper, whose due observance he makes both a sign and a means of purity in churches.

debates.question: Why was the ark not in its place?

positions.position: It had been removed from the inner sanctuary, probably under one of the idolatrous kings.
The priests had hidden it for safety and can now restore it.
The verse is not about a displaced ark at all but relieves the Levites of carrying it, now that it has a fixed place.

4.pericope_label: And prepare yourselves by the houses of your fathers, after your courses, according to the writing of David king of Israel, and according to the writing of Solomon his son. And stand in the holy place according to the divisions of the families of the fathers of your brethren the people, and after the division of the families of the Levites. So kill the passover, and sanctify yourselves, and prepare your brethren, that they may do according to the word of the Lord by the hand of Moses. And Josiah gave to the people, of the flock, lambs and kids, all for the passover offerings, for all that were present, to the number of thirty thousand, and three thousand bullocks: these were of the king’s substance.

schools.summary: Ellicott sets out the arrangement by which a portion of a Levitical father-house was stationed beside every whole house of laymen, and lists what the service consisted of — killing and skinning the lambs, handing the blood to the priests, giving the people their share of the roasted flesh; Delitzsch states the upshot as serving your brethren the laymen, and explains the odd placing of the sanctifying between the killing and the preparing as the washing required before the blood was handed to the priest.

Gill reads the command to prepare as a charge to be ready, diligent, and exact to the law, places the standing in the court of the priests, and counts the thirty thousand lambs and kids as enough to serve thirty thousand households.
Wesley notes that the verb rendered stand frequently carries the sense of ministering rather than merely being present.

themes: And prepare yourselves by the houses of your fathers, after your courses, according to the writing of David king of Israel, and according to the writing of Solomon his son.
And stand in the holy place according to the divisions of the families of the fathers of your brethren the people, and after the division of the families of the Levites.
So kill the passover, and sanctify yourselves, and prepare your brethren, that they may do according to the word of the Lord by the hand of Moses.

And Josiah gave to the people, of the flock, lambs and kids, all for the passover offerings, for all that were present, to the number of thirty thousand, and three thousand bullocks: these were of the king’s substance.

8.pericope_label: And his princes gave willingly unto the people, to the priests, and to the Levites: Hilkiah and Zechariah and Jehiel, rulers of the house of God, gave unto the priests for the passover offerings two thousand and six hundred small cattle, and three hundred oxen. Conaniah also, and Shemaiah and Nethaneel, his brethren, and Hashabiah and Jeiel and Jozabad, chief of the Levites, gave unto the Levites for passover offerings five thousand small cattle, and five hundred oxen. So the service was prepared, and the priests stood in their place, and the Levites in their courses, according to the king’s commandment.

schools.summary: Delitzsch takes the same word for the princes of the kingdom, the king's own great men, reads the key term as naming a freewill offering rather than describing the manner of giving, and marks the summary verse as the hinge where what was arranged is carried out; Ellicott renders the summary as the preparations being completed and the priests' place as their station.

Gill takes the princes who gave to be ecclesiastical rather than secular, reading the names that follow as proof, observes that their gift reached poor priests and Levites whom the king's bounty had not covered, and says everything was made ready for the passover and for the unleavened bread together, for rich and poor alike.

debates.question: Who were the princes that gave?

positions.position: Ecclesiastical princes — rulers of the house of God, as the names that follow show.
The princes of the kingdom, the king’s own great men.

themes: And his princes gave willingly unto the people, to the priests, and to the Levites: Hilkiah and Zechariah and Jehiel, rulers of the house of God, gave unto the priests for the passover offerings two thousand and six hundred small cattle, and three hundred oxen.

Conaniah also, and Shemaiah and Nethaneel, his brethren, and Hashabiah and Jeiel and Jozabad, chief of the Levites, gave unto the Levites for passover offerings five thousand small cattle, and five hundred oxen.

11.pericope_label: And they killed the passover, and the priests sprinkled the blood from their hands, and the Levites flayed them. And they removed the burnt offerings, that they might give according to the divisions of the families of the people, to offer unto the Lord, as it is written in the book of Moses. And so did they with the oxen. And they roasted the passover with fire according to the ordinance: but the other holy offerings sod they in pots, and in caldrons, and in pans, and divided them speedily among all the people.

schools.summary: Delitzsch traces the relay by which Levites slew, priests sprinkled the blood handed them, and Levites flayed, and identifies the consecrated things boiled in pots as the oxen; Ellicott explains the singular hand as the Levites' own, observes that what had been an exception under Hezekiah has here become the rule, takes the removed portions as the pieces due to the altar although no burnt offering proper was appointed for the passover evening, and stresses the haste with which the cooked meat was carried out to the laity.

Gill has the Levites do the killing, allows two senses for what was removed — either the animals set aside for burnt offerings or the portions taken out of each to be burnt, the fat of the inwards, the kidneys, the caul on the liver — and anchors the roasting in the ordinance given by Moses.

themes: And they killed the passover, and the priests sprinkled the blood from their hands, and the Levites flayed them.

And they removed the burnt offerings, that they might give according to the divisions of the families of the people, to offer unto the Lord, as it is written in the book of Moses. And so did they with the oxen.
And they roasted the passover with fire according to the ordinance: but the other holy offerings sod they in pots, and in caldrons, and in pans, and divided them speedily among all the people.

14.pericope_label: And afterward they made ready for themselves, and for the priests: because the priests the sons of Aaron were busied in offering of burnt offerings and the fat until night; therefore the Levites prepared for themselves, and for the priests the sons of Aaron. And the singers the sons of Asaph were in their place, according to the commandment of David, and Asaph, and Heman, and Jeduthun the king’s seer; and the porters waited at every gate; they might not depart from their service; for their brethren the Levites prepared for them. So all the service of the Lord was prepared the same day, to keep the passover, and to offer burnt offerings upon the altar of the Lord, according to the commandment of king Josiah. And the children of Israel that were present kept the passover at that time, and the feast of unleavened bread seven days.

schools.summary: Delitzsch explains that the priests had to be waited on because they were occupied with the burnt offerings and the fat until nightfall, records that the porters could not leave their gates and were therefore provisioned by their brethren, and adds the seven days of unleavened bread from the fifteenth to the twenty-first; Ellicott reads the same day as meaning at that time and explains the burnt offerings of the summary as the burning of the fat.

Gill notes that the Levites served themselves and the priests only afterwards, and places the singers in the court of the priests, playing while the sacrifices were offered; he fixes the passover on the fourteenth of Nisan.

themes: And afterward they made ready for themselves, and for the priests: because the priests the sons of Aaron were busied in offering of burnt offerings and the fat until night; therefore the Levites prepared for themselves, and for the priests the sons of Aaron.

18.pericope_label: And there was no passover like to that kept in Israel from the days of Samuel the prophet; neither did all the kings of Israel keep such a passover as Josiah kept, and the priests, and the Levites, and all Judah and Israel that were present, and the inhabitants of Jerusalem. In the eighteenth year of the reign of Josiah was this passover kept.

schools.summary: Delitzsch notes that this book dates the comparison from the days of Samuel where the older account reaches back to the judges, reads the closing enumeration from king down to the inhabitants of Jerusalem as deliberate rhetoric performing the universality it claims, and draws out a difference between the two histories at the turn to Josiah's death: the older book prefaces the catastrophe with the statement that God did not turn from his wrath against Judah because of the sins of Manasseh, and this book does not.

Gill itemises what earned the superlative — the feast kept so exactly to the law, so universally by Israel and Judah together, and with such liberality from the king and the chief men of the priests and Levites.

themes: And there was no passover like to that kept in Israel from the days of Samuel the prophet; neither did all the kings of Israel keep such a passover as Josiah kept, and the priests, and the Levites, and all Judah and Israel that were present, and the inhabitants of Jerusalem.
In the eighteenth year of the reign of Josiah was this passover kept.

20.pericope_label: After all this, when Josiah had prepared the temple, Necho king of Egypt came up to fight against Carchemish by Euphrates: and Josiah went out against him. But he sent ambassadors to him, saying, What have I to do with thee, thou king of Judah? I come not against thee this day, but against the house wherewith I have war: for God commanded me to make haste: forbear thee from meddling with God, who is with me, that he destroy thee not. Nevertheless Josiah would not turn his face from him, but disguised himself, that he might fight with him, and hearkened not unto the words of Necho from the mouth of God, and came to fight in the valley of Megiddo.

schools.summary: Delitzsch corrects the phrase about the house of Necho's war, which means the hereditary enemy rather than a warlike house, and reads the verb describing Josiah's disguise as carrying a moral sense as well as a sartorial one — to disfigure oneself, to undertake what contradicts one's own character, which is what a king who had spent his reign carrying out God's will did in resisting a word claiming to come from God.

Gill lists what had just been achieved — the temple purified, repaired, its service put on a good footing — and says prosperity might reasonably have been expected after it; on the king's refusal he says plainly that he would not withdraw his forces and go back.

Henry counts the thirteen years between the passover and the death and asks why the narrative passes them in silence, answering that the people were not turned from the love of their sins nor God from the fierceness of his anger, so that the next news of Josiah is that he is cut off in the midst of his days and usefulness before he is forty.

outliers.claim: That the verb describing Josiah's disguise is transferred to the moral realm, so that in disguising his person the king also disfigured his character — the one action of the reign that contradicted it.

themes: After all this, when Josiah had prepared the temple, Necho king of Egypt came up to fight against Carchemish by Euphrates: and Josiah went out against him.

23.pericope_label: And the archers shot at king Josiah; and the king said to his servants, Have me away; for I am sore wounded. His servants therefore took him out of that chariot, and put him in the second chariot that he had; and they brought him to Jerusalem, and he died, and was buried in one of the sepulchres of his fathers. And all Judah and Jerusalem mourned for Josiah. And Jeremiah lamented for Josiah: and all the singing men and the singing women spake of Josiah in their lamentations to this day, and made them an ordinance in Israel: and, behold, they are written in the lamentations.

schools.summary: Ellicott sets this account of the death beside the older one, which has the servants make him ride dead or dying from Megiddo, and refuses the suggestion that this chapter is an arbitrary literary alteration of it, arguing that the divergence points instead to the chronicler having material of his own.

Gill explains that the disguise concealed the king but not the commander, so that a man evidently in chief command drew the archers' fire, reports that they brought him to Jerusalem and buried him there, and guards against a common misidentification of Jeremiah's lost lamentation, which is not the passage sometimes cited for it.

Clarke offers a flat explanation of the second chariot, that they moved him out of his own either for secrecy or because it had been disabled, and widens the frame on the lamentation, noting that the Hebrews had poetical compositions for every great occasion and that this one has simply not survived; he passes on the Targum's account of an annual mourning.

themes: And the archers shot at king Josiah; and the king said to his servants, Have me away; for I am sore wounded.

26.pericope_label: Now the rest of the acts of Josiah, and his goodness, according to that which was written in the law of the Lord, And his deeds, first and last, behold, they are written in the book of the kings of Israel and Judah.

schools.summary: Ellicott points out that the goodness here is said to be according to what is written in the law of the Lord, a measurement made of no other king, and notes the wider title this book gives its source, the kings of Israel and Judah where the older account names Judah alone.
Gill sums the closing formula in two words, the king's piety toward God and his liberality to the people.

Clarke passes on the Targum's expansion of the phrase about first and last deeds, which reads like a table of contents for a book nobody has, and observes plainly that these general histories are lost and that what survives of the leading facts is what stands in the books we possess.

themes: Now the rest of the acts of Josiah, and his goodness, according to that which was written in the law of the Lord,
And his deeds, first and last, behold, they are written in the book of the kings of Israel and Judah.
